O R D E R
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
IA NO.595 OF 2026
(For condonation of delay in filing appeal)
1. This application has been filed by the appellant seeking condonation
of delay in filing the appeal.
2. Facts and circumstances of the case leading to the filing of the instant
appeal which are relevant for the disposal of the present application are
undisputed and are narrated hereinbelow: -
(a) The appeal is directed against the three orders passed by the 1st
respondent Tamil Nadu Electricity Regulatory Commission
(hereinafter referred to as “the Commission”) i.e. order dated
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 2 of 22

09.07.2024 passed in MP No.28/2023 (in short “first impugned
order”), order dated 28.01.2025 passed in RP No.2/2024 (in short
“second impugned order”) and order dated 17.02.2026 passed in
MP No.41/2025 (in short “third impugned order”).
(b) The respondent no.2 Techno Electric and Engineering Company
Limited, a wind power generator with a total installed capacity of
111.90 MW in the State of Tamil Nadu, had filed a petition bearing
MP No.28/2023 before the Commission challenging the circular
dated 01.04.2022 issued by appellant, the distribution licensee in
the State of Tamil Nadu, through which Average Power Purchase
Cost (APPC) was capped at 75% of the discovered price for wind
energy at Rs.2.69/unit as notified by Solar Energy Corporation of
India (SECI) i.e. the tariff discovered under Section 63 of the
Electricity Act, 2003.
(c) The petition was disposed of by the Commission vide order dated
09.07.2024 (first impugned order) holding the following in favour of
2nd respondent: -
(i) 75% cap cannot be applied on APPC considering bid
discovered tariff;
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 3 of 22

(ii) Directed the appellant to pay tariff to 2nd respondent at full
APPC rate without applying any cap whenever APPC rate
does not breach the preferential tariff; and
(iii) Whenever APPC rate breaches the preferential tariff, the
appellant shall make payments to 2nd respondent at 75% of
the preferential tariff.
(d) The 2nd respondent filed review petition bearing No.2/2024 on
06.08.2024 before the Commission seeking review of the above
noted first impugned order dated 09.07.2024 on the limited issue
that the Commission linked and compared APPC with preferential
tariff for the control period in which the Renewable Energy (RE)
plant was commissioned i.e. the “commissioning year” instead of
“corresponding year”.
(e) The review petition was allowed by the Commission vide order
dated 28.01.2025 (second impugned order) thereby holding that the
cap on APPC would arise in the year in which the APPC rate
crosses over preferential tariff of the “corresponding year” and not
the year of commissioning of the RE plant.
(f) During the pendency of the review petition before the Commission,
the appellant had already filed appeal no.131/2025 in this Tribunal
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 4 of 22

challenging the first impugned order dated 09.07.2024 contending,
inter alia, that:
(i) bid discovered tariff can be considered for capping APPC in
absence of preferential tariff; and
(ii) for comparing APPC, preferential tariff of the “corresponding
year” has to be considered instead of “commissioning year” of
the RE plant.
(g) Manifestly, the contention no.(ii) raised in the appeal was addressed
by the Commission in the review order dated 28.01.2025, as noted
hereinabove.
(h) While the said appeal filed by the appellant was pending before this
Tribunal, the appellant filed a petition before the Commission
bearing MP No.41/2025 seeking clarification of the review order
dated 28.01.2025. The petition was filed in the month of June,
2025.
(i) Subsequent to filing of the clarification petition before the
Commission, the appellant withdrew the appeal no.131/2025 from
this Tribunal on 16.09.2025 in view of the pendency of the
clarification petition before the Commission. The appellant had also
sought liberty to reagitate the issue, if necessary, after culmination
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 5 of 22

of the proceedings in clarification petition bearing MP No.41/2025
before the Commission and accordingly, such liberty was granted
by this Tribunal.
(j) The clarification petition of the appellant was dismissed by the
Commission vide order dated 17.02.2026 (third impugned order)
holding that the issue with respect to comparison of the APPC with
the tariff discovered through competitive bidding had already been
conclusively decided in its earlier order dated 09.07.2024 (first
impugned order) and that the Commission had become functus
officio and therefore, could not reopen or rewrite its earlier decision
by way of clarifications.
(k) Accordingly, the appellant has approached this Tribunal again by
way of instant appeal purportedly in terms of the liberty granted by
this Tribunal vide order dated 16.09.2025 while dismissing the
appellant’s earlier appeal no.131/2025.
3. Thus, there has been a delay of 632 days in challenging the first
impugned order, whereas the delay in challenging the second impugned
order stands at 424 days. Such period of delay includes the period of 45
days from the date on which the impugned orders had been passed.
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 6 of 22

4. We have heard Mr. B.P. Patil, learned senior counsel appearing on
behalf of the appellant and Mr. Sajan Poovayya, learned senior counsel
appearing on behalf of the 2nd respondent. We have also perused the
impugned orders, the application for condonation of delay as well as the reply
to the same filed by the 2nd respondent.
5. Learned senior counsel for the appellant argued that the cause of
action to approach this Tribunal by way of instant appeal arose only upon
dismissal of the clarification petition by the Commission vide order dated
17.02.2026 whereby the Commission declined to examine the substantive
issue raised by the appellant on the ground that it had become functus officio.
He would submit strenuously that the delay in filing the appeal has neither
been intentional nor deliberate but has occurred only on account of bonafide
and diligent pursuit of remedies by the appellant before the Commission
including the proceedings of the clarification petition. Thus, on these
submissions, the learned senior counsel urged this Tribunal to condone the
delay in filing the appeal.
6. Per contra, on behalf of 2nd respondent, it is argued by the learned
senior counsel that by filing the clarification petition before the Commission
during the pendency of the earlier appeal no.31/2025, the appellant has
indulged in forum shopping and thus, has abused the process of law. It is
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 7 of 22

argued that even if the issues raised in the clarification petition were identical
to the issues dealt by the Commission in the first and second impugned
orders, the clarification petition was not an extension of the proceedings that
culminated in passing of first and second impugned orders. It is pointed out
that the clarification petition was a fresh petition and since the appellant could
not obtain desired reliefs in the same from the Commission, it misused the
liberty granted by this Tribunal by filing instant fresh appeal. Learned senior
counsel would further argue that liberty granted by this Tribunal does not
render the instant fresh appeal maintainable and does not save it from law
of limitation. In this regard, he has relied upon the judgment of the Hon'ble
Supreme Court in Arifa v. Abhiman Apartment Cooperative Housing Society
Ltd., (2025) 10 SCC 700. Learned senior counsel also cited the order of this
Tribunal dated 15.01.2026 in DFR No.315/2025 in TNPDCL v. TNERC &
Ors. to canvas that this Tribunal has time and again been refusing to
condone the delay of more than one year in filing the appeals. Accordingly,
the learned senior counsel urged us to dismiss the application.
7. We have given a thoughtful consideration to the rival submissions
made by the learned senior counsels.
8. Sub-section 2 of Section 111 of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides that
every appeal shall be filed in this Tribunal within a period of 45 days from the
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 8 of 22

date on which the copy of the impugned order is received by the aggrieved
person i.e. the appellant. Proviso attached to this sub-section empowers this
Tribunal to entertain an appeal after the expiry of the said period of 45 days
if this Tribunal is satisfied that the appellant was prevented by “sufficient
cause” from filing the appeal within the prescribed period of 45 days. This
proviso attached to Section 111(2) of the Act is in pari materia with Section
5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, which provides that any appeal or any
application may be admitted after the prescribed period, if the appellant or
applicant satisfies the court that he had “sufficient cause” for not preferring
the appeal or making the application within such period.
9. The words “sufficient cause” had come up for interpretation before the
Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shivamma (Dead) by LRs v. Karnataka Housing
Board & Ors., 2025 INSC 1104. Paragraph Nos.23 and 40 of the judgment
are material for our discussion and are extracted hereinbelow: -
“23. In Ramkumar Choudhary (supra), this very Bench
had the occasion to examine the meaning of the expression
“within such period” used in Section 5 of the Limitation Act.
Placing reliance on the decisions of this Court in Ajit Singh
Thakur (supra) and Basawaraj (supra), it was held that for the
purpose of Section 5, the party seeking condonation of delay
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 9 of 22

has to explain why it was unable to institute the proceedings
within the prescribed period of limitation. Events that occurred
after the expiry of the period of limitation till the date of actual
filing of the appeal or application, as the case may be, would
be of no consequence insofar as condonation is concerned, if
it is unable to explain what came in the way of the party that it
was unable to file it. It reiterated that no event or circumstance
arising after the expiry of limitation can constitute such
sufficient cause, where the party allowed the limitation to expiry
unless it can trace such failure in allowing the limitation to
expire to a cause arising within the period of limitation. The
relevant observations read as under:-
…..
40. As such, under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, for the
purpose of seeking condonation of delay in filing of an appeal
or application, as the case may be, beyond the stipulated
period of limitation, the delay in the filing has to be explained
by demonstrating the existence of a “sufficient cause” that
resulted in such delay for both the prescribed period of
limitation as-well as the period after the expiry of limitation, up
to actual date of filing of such appeal or application, as the case
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 10 of 22

may be, or to put it simply, explanation has to be given for the
entire duration from the date when the clock of limitation began
to tick, up until the date of actual filing, for seeking condonation
of delay by recourse to Section 5 of the Limitation Act.”
10. Thus, in view of the legal principle enunciated in the above referred
Paragraphs of the judgment, while citing with approval the earlier judgments
in Ramkumar Choudhary’s case and Basawaraj’s case, the delay in filing
has to be explained by demonstrating existence of “sufficient cause” that
prevented the appellants from filing the appeal both within the prescribed
period of limitation as well as the period after the expiry of limitation period
up to the actual date of filing. However, Paragraphs 136 and 137 of the
judgment are also material and are extracted hereinbelow: -
“136 When technical considerations of limitation conflict
with the imperative of substantial justice, the latter should
ordinarily prevail. Rules of limitation are not designed to destroy
the rights of parties but to prevent inordinate delay in seeking
remedies. Thus, the interpretation of “sufficient cause” must be
liberal and purposive, aimed at advancing the cause of justice
rather than defeating it. This is why the courts, while construing
applications for condonation of delay, emphasize the bona
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 11 of 22

fides of the applicant over the sheer arithmetical length of the
delay.
137. Where strict adherence to these rules results in
injustice, the Court is dutybound to apply a liberal interpretation
of “sufficient cause” so as to balance technical requirements
with the demands of justice. A litigant does not stand to benefit
by lodging an appeal late, and therefore, a pragmatic and
justice-oriented approach must inform the judicial discretion
under Section 5. This decision continues to be the most
frequently cited authority for the proposition that the judiciary
should incline towards justice rather than technicality.
Therefore, when courts interpret “sufficient cause,” they are
expected to exercise discretion in a manner that fosters justice,
fairness, and equity, keeping in mind the realities of litigation.”
11. Thus, while deciding an application for condonation of delay, the courts
are duty bound to give a liberal interpretation to the term “sufficient cause” in
order to balance the technical requirements with the demands of justice and
are expected to exercise discretion in a manner that fosters justice, fairness
and equity, while keeping in mind realities of litigation.
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 12 of 22

12. In the case of Maniben Devraj Shah v. Municipal Corporation of Brihan
Mumbai, (2012) 5 SCC 157 also, the Supreme Court has advocated liberal
and justice oriented approach in exercise of power under Section 5 of the
Limitation Act and other similar statutes but has cautioned that courts cannot
be oblivious of the fact that a successful litigant has acquired certain rights
on the basis of the judgment under challenge and a lot of time has been
consumed at various stages of litigation apart from the costs. The judgment
laid down the principle that if the courts find that there has been no
negligence on the part of the appellant and the cause shown for delay does
not lack bonafides, then it may condone the delay but on the other hand, if
the explanation given by the applicant is found to be concocted or he has
been thoroughly negligent in prosecuting his case, it would be a legitimate
exercise of discretion not to condone the delay.
13. In the case of Isha Bhattacharjee v. Managing Committee of
Raghunathpur Nafar Academy (2013) 12 SCC 649, the Apex Court has
enunciated following principles to be kept in mind while deciding an
application for condonation of delay: -
“i) There should be a liberal, pragmatic, justice-oriented, non-
pedantic approach while dealing with an application for
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 13 of 22

condonation of delay, for the courts are not supposed to
legalise injustice but are obliged to remove injustice.
ii) The terms sufficient cause should be understood in their
proper spirit, philosophy and purpose regard being had to the
fact that these terms are basically elastic and are to be applied
in proper perspective to the obtaining fact-situation.
iii) Substantial justice being paramount and pivotal the technical
considerations should not be given undue and uncalled for
emphasis.
iv) No presumption can be attached to deliberate causation of
delay but, gross negligence on the part of the counsel or litigant
is to be taken note of.
v) Lack of bona fides imputable to a party seeking condonation
of delay is a significant and relevant fact.
vi) It is to be kept in mind that adherence to strict proof should
not affect public justice and cause public mischief because the
courts are required to be vigilant so that in the ultimate
eventuate there is no real failure of justice.
vii) The concept of liberal approach has to encapsule the
conception of reasonableness and it cannot be allowed a totally
unfettered free play.
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 14 of 22

viii) There is a distinction between inordinate delay and a
delay of short duration or few days, for to the former doctrine of
prejudice is attracted whereas to the latter it may not be
attracted. That apart, the first one warrants strict approach
whereas the second calls for a liberal delineation.
ix) The conduct, behaviour and attitude of a party relating to its
inaction or negligence are relevant factors to be taken into
consideration. It is so as the fundamental principle is that the
courts are required to weigh the scale of balance of justice in
respect of both parties and the said principle cannot be given a
total go by in the name of liberal approach.
x) If the explanation offered is concocted or the grounds urged
in the application are fanciful, the courts should be vigilant not
to expose the other side unnecessarily to face such a litigation.
xi) It is to be borne in mind that no one gets away with fraud,
misrepresentation or interpolation by taking recourse to the
technicalities of law of limitation.
xii) The entire gamut of facts are to be carefully scrutinized
and the approach should be based on the paradigm of judicial
discretion which is founded on objective reasoning and not on
individual perception.
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 15 of 22

xiii) The State or a public body or an entity representing a
collective cause should be given some acceptable latitude.”
14. In the instant case, the appellant had already assailed the first
impugned order dated 09.07.2024 before this Tribunal by way of appeal
no.131/2025. The same had been filed during the pendency of the review
petition filed by the 2nd respondent before the Commission. The review
petition came to be allowed by the Commission vide second impugned order
dated 28.01.2025. Subsequent to the passing of the said order dated
28.01.2025 by the Commission, the appellant filed petition bearing MP
No.41/2025 before the Commission seeking clarification of the said review
order. Thereafter, the appellant approached this Tribunal with a prayer for
withdrawal of the appeal no.131/2025 in view of the pendency of the
clarification petition before the Commission with liberty to reagitate the
issues raised in the appeal afresh after culmination of the proceedings in the
clarification petition, if need so arose. Accordingly, the appeal was dismissed
as withdrawn while granting such liberty to the appellant.
15. The clarification petition came to be dismissed by the Commission vide
third impugned order dated 17.02.2026. Upon such dismissal of the
clarification petition, the appellant filed the instant appeal purportedly in
terms of the liberty granted by this Tribunal vide order dated 16.09.2025
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 16 of 22

while dismissing the appellant’s earlier appeal no.131/2025. Undisputedly,
the instant appeal has been filed within the statutory period of 45 days from
the date of dismissal of the clarification petition i.e. 17.02.2026, as prescribed
in the Electricity Act, 2003 for filing of appeal before this Tribunal.
16. The aforesaid facts and circumstances in which the present appeal has
been filed by the appellant, albeit with a delay, do not demonstrate that there
has been any negligence on the part of the appellant or that its conduct
exhibits lack of bonafides. It is evident that the 2nd respondent itself was not
satisfied with the first impugned order dated 09.07.2024 and accordingly filed
review petition no.2/2024 before the Commission seeking review of the said
order, even though on a limited issue. While the review proceedings were
going on, the appellant approached this Tribunal by way of appeal
no.131/2025 thereby assailing the said first impugned order dated
09.07.2024. After the filing of the said appeal by the appellant, the
Commission allowed the review petition filed by the 2nd respondent vide
second impugned order dated 28.01.2025 which order addressed one of the
contentions of the appellant also raised in the said appeal. Accordingly, the
appellant appears to have been advised to seek clarification about the said
review order dated 28.01.2025 from the Commission and hence, it filed a
clarification petition before the Commission. The appellant probably was
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 17 of 22

under the impression that the Commission would issue the clarifications as
sought by the appellant and accordingly, withdrew the appeal no.131/2025
from this Tribunal with liberty to file a fresh appeal after the culmination of
proceedings of the clarification petition.
17. As already noted hereinabove, the instant appeal has been filed in
terms of the said liberty granted by this Tribunal to the appellant vide order
dated 16.09.2025.
18. It is true that as per the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the
case of Arifa v. Abhiman Apartment Cooperative Housing Society Limited
(supra), where suit or an appeal is withdrawn with the leave of court to file
fresh suit or appeal, the law of limitation applies with full force in view of Rule
2 of Order 23 of CPC and such an order does not save limitation for filing the
fresh appeal. Securing liberty from the appellate court does not
automatically stop or extend the statutory limitation period. It does not freeze
the limitation period for new proceedings. It is for this reason only that the
appellant has filed the present application along with the instant appeal for
condonation of delay in filing the appeal, which we are proposing to dispose
of by way of this order. The appellant has not sought condonation of delay
as of right by virtue of the order dated 16.09.2025 of this Tribunal vide which
its earlier appeal was dismissed as withdrawn with liberty to the appellant to
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 18 of 22

file a fresh appeal. The appellant has set out the facts and circumstances,
as noted hereinabove, which led it to withdraw the earlier appeal
no.131/2025 and thereafter to file the instant appeal afresh in terms of the
liberty granted to it.
19. The reference on the part of the second respondent to the order dated
15.01.2026 of the Tribunal in DFR No.315/2025 is misplaced for the reason
that this Tribunal has not laid down a general principle in that order to the
effect that delay in filing an appeal beyond period of one year cannot be
condoned in any circumstances. Such a principle, even if laid down, would
be contrary to Section 111(2) of the Electricity Act, 2003 as well as Section
5 of the Limitation Act which do not specify any period beyond which delay
cannot be condoned. These two legal provisions only envisages that delay
can be and must be condoned only where the appellant demonstrates
“sufficient cause” which prevented it from filing the appeal within the
prescribed period of limitation. In the said referred case, this Tribunal
refused to condone delay having regard to the facts and circumstances in
which that appeal had been filed which are totally distinct from the facts and
circumstances in which the instant appeal has been filed by the appellant
herein.
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 19 of 22

20. Even though, the delay in filing the instant appeal by the appellant,
when computed from the date of the first impugned order i.e. 09.07.2024, is
long enough but by no stretch of imagination can it be said to be so inordinate
or contumacious that it cannot be condoned. Having regard to the conduct
of the appellant throughout, it is evident that the appellant was not sitting idle
but had been taking steps to assail the Commission’s orders by way of
different proceedings either before this Tribunal or before the Commission
itself. Therefore, no negligence or inaction can be imputed to the appellant.
The reasons for delay agitated by the appellant cannot be said to be
concocted or fanciful. The entire gamut of facts and circumstances that have
taken place after the passing of first impugned order dated 09.07.2024 by
the Commission, when scrutinized in the light of legal principles enunciated
by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in above referred judgments, leads to only
conclusion that the delay in filing the appeal on the part of the appellant is
neither deliberate nor inordinate so as to warrant dismissal of the application
under consideration.
21. We are not impressed with the submissions of the learned senior
counsel appearing for the 2nd respondent that by approaching the
Commission with a petition for clarification of the review order dated
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 20 of 22

28.01.2025 during the pendency of the earlier appeal no.131/2025, the
appellant has resorted to forum shopping. The appellant had withdrawn the
appeal no.131/2025 purportedly with the hope that he may succeed in the
clarification petition before the Commission as one of its grievances had
been addressed in the said review order dated 28.01.2025. As an abundant
caution the appellant had sought (and was granted) liberty to file a fresh
appeal after the culmination of the proceedings of the clarification petition, if
need so arose. The appellant could not have continued the proceedings of
the appeal no.131/2025 as well as the clarification petition at the same time.
Therefore, it is clearly not a case of forum shopping. Had it been so, this
Tribunal would not have granted liberty, as noted hereinabove, to the
appellant at the time of dismissal as withdrawn of the appeal no.131/2025
vide order dated 16.09.2025.
22. Hence, adopting the liberal and purposive interpretation of the term
“sufficient cause” as advocated by the Apex Court in the case of Shivamma
(supra), we are of the opinion that the demands of justice would be met in
case the delay in filing the appeal is condoned subject to payment of costs.
23. Therefore, the instant application is hereby allowed and delay in filing
the appeal is condoned subject to appellant paying costs of Rs.50,000/-
____________________________________________________________________________________
IA No.595/2026 in DFR No.154/2026 Page 21 of 22

(Rupees fifty thousand only) to second respondent M/s Techno Electric and
Engineering Company Limited within two weeks from today. Needless to
add that in case of failure to pay such costs within the stipulated period, the
appeal shall stand dismissed as time barred.
DFR NO.154 OF 2026 &
IA NO.596 OF 2026
24. Let replies to the appeal as well as the application for interim relief be
filed by the respondents within four weeks. The appellant shall file rejoinder,
if any, within two weeks thereafter.
25. List the matter on 28.09.2026.
Pronounced in the open court on this the 10th day of August, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson
